problem: The conversion from φ to the standard drag coefficient is wrong by a factor. With A = πD²/4, the denominator ½ρV²A equals ρV²πD²/8, so C_D = F/(½ρV²A) = 8φ/π, not (π/2)φ. The stated (π/2)φ ≈ 1.57φ understates it; the correct factor is 8/π ≈ 2.55.
fix: C_D = F/(½ρV²A) = (8/π) φ(Re), a function of Reynolds number alone.

problem: "a dimensionless constant forces every exponent to sum to zero" is wrong and will mislead. Nothing sums to zero: the constant C simply contributes no M, L or T, so it drops out of the exponent equations. What you actually do is equate the M, L and T exponents of the two sides.
fix: Equate exponents of M, L and T on the two sides. The constant C is dimensionless, so it adds no exponents to the right-hand side.

problem: "Two variables that are physically linked can be tested for a link using dimensions alone" is loose: dimensional analysis cannot discover or test whether a link exists. The variable list is a physical judgement supplied by the engineer; dimensions only fix the form of the relation.
fix: "Once you have decided which variables matter, dimensions alone fix the form of the relation between them, up to an unknown function."

problem: F/(ρV²D²) is called "a drag coefficient", but step 7 of the worked example shows the usual drag coefficient is F/(½ρV²A), which differs by the factor 8/π. A student may take the two as the same quantity.
fix: "F/(ρV²D²) has the form of a drag coefficient — force divided by area, then by ρV² — and differs from the standard C_D only by a constant factor (8/π)."
